notes.meaning: David is amazed that earthly nations and their peoples make angry plans against God. Their rebellion is completely useless because no human power can stop the Lord's plans.

Rulers and kings join forces to stand together in open revolt against the Lord and His chosen King. The word Anointed means the Messiah, God's chosen deliverer Jesus Christ, so fighting the King means fighting God Himself.
The rebellious leaders openly declare that they want to throw off God's authority. They treat God's holy laws like prison chains and ropes that hold them back from doing whatever they want.
God stays calmly seated on His throne in heaven, undisturbed by human arrogance. He looks down with contempt and laughs at their powerless attempts to defeat Him.
The Lord breaks His silence to speak directly to the rebels in righteous fury. His terrifying words show that He will judge their pride and bring their plans to nothing.
God announces that He has already placed His royal King on Mount Zion in Jerusalem. While this first applied to King David, it points forward to Jesus Christ, who reigns forever over God's people.
The chosen King speaks, declaring the official decree given to Him by the Lord. God declared Him to be His royal Son, a promise made to David's royal line and fulfilled when Jesus rose from the dead.
The Father invites His Son to ask for the whole world as His royal inheritance. His rule is not limited to Israel, because every nation on earth belongs to Christ by right.
The King has absolute power to shatter those who stubbornly fight against His rule. Those who reject His mercy will be broken as easily as an iron rod smashes a clay pot.
Earthly kings and judges are urged to show good sense while there is still time. True wisdom means dropping their pride, taking God's warning to heart, and turning back to Him.
All rulers and subjects are told to serve the Lord with deep awe and reverence. Living under God brings real happiness, but worship must always keep a healthy respect for His holiness.
The rulers are commanded to kiss the Son as a sign of loyal submission and love. Refusing Him brings sudden ruin under His wrath, but everyone who runs to Him for safety finds true blessing.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient Greek and Latin translations render this phrase as giving pure homage or accepting instruction rather than kissing the Son.
